title: Shoemaker v. United States (1893)
summary: Congress may give new duties to officers who already hold appointed and confirmed offices without a fresh appointment, as long as the new duties are germane to the old office.
notes:
Key line: Congress may increase the duties of an existing office without rendering it necessary that the incumbent should be again nominated, confirmed and appointed. (Justice Shiras, syllabus statement of the holding)

Citation: 147 U.S. 282 (1893).

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs in error were Shoemaker and other owners of land along Rock Creek in the District of Columbia whose tracts had been condemned for Rock Creek Park. The defendant in error was the United States, acting through the commission that the Act of September 27, 1890 created to select and acquire the park land. The commission had five members: the Chief of Engineers of the United States Army, the Engineer Commissioner of the District of Columbia, and three citizens appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. The landowners challenged the commission's composition, the taking, the valuation and the assessment of benefits.
sections.Material Facts: By the Act of September 27, 1890, 26 Stat. 492, Congress directed that a tract of not more than two thousand acres on both sides of Rock Creek be dedicated as a public park. The commission was to select the land, survey it, and file a map, which it recorded on April 16, 1891; from that date the parcels were held as condemned, subject to just compensation. If the commission could not agree with owners on a price approved by the President within thirty days, it was to petition the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia, which would appoint three disinterested appraisers. The appraised values would be paid if the President found them reasonable. The Act also let the court assess part of the cost on neighboring property specially benefited. The Chief of Engineers and the Engineer Commissioner sat on the commission by virtue of their existing offices, without new nominations or confirmations.
sections.Procedural History: The commission petitioned the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia for an assessment of the value of parcels it could not buy by agreement. The court appointed appraisers, received their report, heard the owners' many objections, including that the commission was unconstitutionally composed, that the taking for a park was not a public use, that the President's approval of prices was a judicial act, and that the appraisers had erred, and overruled them in written opinions. It confirmed the report. The owners brought a writ of error to the Supreme Court of the United States, which heard argument on November 28 and 29, 1892, decided the case on January 16, 1893, and affirmed. Justice Shiras wrote for the Court.
sections.Issue: For this course the central question was whether Congress violated the Appointments Clause by making the Chief of Engineers of the Army and the Engineer Commissioner of the District of Columbia members of the Rock Creek Park commission without a new presidential nomination and Senate confirmation for the new position. The Court also decided whether taking land for a public park is a public use, whether the President's approval of the price to be paid was a judicial function improperly given to the Executive, whether the Act's aggregate cost limit bound the appraisers on individual parcels, whether benefits could be assessed on nearby property, and whether the appraisers' oath and methods were proper.
sections.Holding: The commission was lawfully composed. The two officers already held offices to which the President had appointed them with Senate confirmation, and the duties of selecting and acquiring park land were germane to those offices, so Congress could add the duties without a second appointment. Taking land for a public park is a public use, and the extent of the taking rests in legislative discretion subject only to just compensation. The President's approval of prices is an executive, not a judicial, act. The aggregate cost limit did not direct appraisers to undervalue particular parcels. Assessing part of the cost on benefited property is permissible. The oath and the appraisers' use of their own inspection along with the evidence were proper, and an appellate court will not disturb their amounts absent gross error. Judgment affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Shiras treated the Appointments Clause objection briefly and directly. The two officers whose eligibility was questioned had been appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate before the Act passed. Congress frequently increases the power and duties of an existing office, and doing so does not require the incumbent to be nominated and confirmed again. The test the Court applied was whether the new duties were germane to the offices already held. Selecting and surveying park land in the federal district is work of the kind an Army engineer and the District's engineer commissioner already performed, so the added duties fit that test. The Court then addressed the remaining objections in the same practical spirit. Parks and squares are public uses, as long practice in cities and States shows, and how much land to take is for the legislature. The proviso in Maryland's act of cession protected private property rights but did not withhold the power of eminent domain that belongs to the United States as sovereign over the District. Presidential approval of a price is a check on expenditure, not adjudication, so no judicial power was misplaced in the Executive. The Act's overall spending cap addressed the commission's total purchases, not the appraisers' judgments of particular parcels. The appraisers could rely on personal inspection as well as testimony, and their report would stand absent proof of prejudice, corruption or plain mistake.

topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: Shoemaker defines when the Appointments Clause requires a fresh appointment for newly assigned duties.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Justice Shiras delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court, and no Justice wrote separately.
